items.title: The Four Candles
items.moral: Moral: When faith, loyalty, and love fade, hope can rekindle them. Keep hope alive, and the others can return.
body: Four candles burned in a room so quiet that their voices could be heard.
The first candle said, “I am FAITH. But no one helps me keep burning. I think I will soon go out.”
Its flame dwindled until it went out altogether.
The second candle said, “I am LOYALTY. Sadly, no one seems to need me anymore. There is no reason for me to keep burning.”
As soon as it finished speaking, a gentle breeze put it out.
The third candle spoke sadly. “I am LOVE. I have no strength left to burn. People have forgotten my worth. They have even forgotten to love those closest to them.”
And with that, LOVE went out too.
Just then, a child entered the room and saw the three dark candles. “Why aren’t you burning? Weren’t you supposed to burn forever?” the child asked, beginning to cry.
The fourth candle spoke. “Don’t be afraid. As long as I am burning, we can light the others again. I am HOPE.”
The child’s eyes brightened. Taking the candle of HOPE, the child relit the others one by one.

items.title: Help Them Yourself, O Exalted Allah!
items.moral: Moral: The last refuge of the helpless, the lonely, and the hopeless is the Creator. Prayer is the language of deepest need.
body: To the restless, left without a home,
to the orphan, left alone,
to the needy, left hungry and thirsty,
to the sick, left in hardship,
to the wounded heart that waits and watches the road,
to the hopeless who can see no way forward,
to the heedless, left without light,
to the one who still has a wish, who still dreams,
to the faithless, left without You —
help them Yourself, O exalted Allah!

items.title: What I Know Now
items.moral: Moral: True maturity is not about changing others, but about knowing who to let into your life and who to stay away from.
body: Reflections from someone who has weathered hard times:
I no longer try to make people love me. Those who do not want to will always find a reason.
I know my worth now. I do not have to prove it to everyone.
I no longer want to spend my life among the arrogant and self-satisfied.
I know that people who truly want something look for a way, while those who do not look for an excuse.
I do not confide in gossips. Anyone who shares other people’s secrets may share mine too.
I no longer try to change the minds of people determined not to listen.
I want distance from people who lie, make empty promises, and fail to keep their word.
I no longer want to be harsh or unforgiving. I value people who can acknowledge a mistake and apologize.
I know I am happiest with people around whom I can be myself.

items.title: A Magnificent Lesson
items.moral: Moral: In education, personal example is stronger than any lecture. A responsible parent may even set aside personal pride to help a child find the right path.
body: As a child, Mehmed the Conqueror, son of the Ottoman Sultan Murad II, would not sit quietly in class and was constantly disruptive. Whenever his teacher, Akşemseddin, corrected him, the boy replied:
“You cannot tell me what to do. I am the sultan’s son!”
Troubled by the boy’s behavior, the teacher hesitated to approach the sultan. At last, he found the courage to explain what was happening.
The sultan thought for a moment and whispered a plan into the teacher’s ear. Akşemseddin protested that it would be impossible, but Murad II insisted:
“It will be done.”
The next day, young Mehmed again misbehaved and answered his teacher with the same threat. At that moment, the sultan opened the door and entered the classroom.
Following the plan, Akşemseddin pretended to be furious. He reprimanded the sultan for entering without permission, even slapped him, and ordered him to leave immediately.
Murad II lowered his head, apologized, and left. Seeing that even his powerful father had to obey the teacher’s rules, the prince was stunned.
A short while later, someone knocked. This time the sultan asked permission to enter and apologized again.
The plan worked. From that day forward, Mehmed no longer disrupted his lessons. For the sake of his son’s upbringing, Murad II had set aside even a ruler’s pride.

items.title: Mihrimah Sultan and Architect Sinan
items.moral: Moral: Being united with the one you love is not always granted. Sometimes a person turns that love into a work that outlives the one who felt it.
body: When Mihrimah Sultan, the daughter of Suleiman the Magnificent, reached the age of seventeen, it is said that two men wished to marry her. One was Rüstem Pasha, the beylerbeyi of Diyarbakır; the other was Architect Sinan, the great master of Ottoman architecture. The name “Mihrimah” is of Persian origin: “mihr” means sun, and “mah” means moon.

Sultan Suleiman married his daughter to Rüstem Pasha. Architect Sinan, already married and approaching fifty, did not see his wish fulfilled. According to the legend, he nevertheless continued to love Mihrimah Sultan deeply.
Unable to share his life with Mihrimah, Sinan is said to have expressed his enduring love through his art.

At the palace’s commission, Architect Sinan built the Mihrimah Sultan Mosque in Üsküdar and turned it into a magnificent architectural monument. Legend says the mosque’s graceful silhouette recalls the lines of a woman whose skirts fall soft to the ground.

Later Sinan raised a second mosque for Mihrimah Sultan at Edirnekapı, one of the highest points in Istanbul. Though relatively compact in scale, it stands out for its exquisite lightness and brightness. Its slender minaret, the many windows ringing the dome, and its refined interior give the mosque a special airiness. Legend holds that some of the patterns and ornaments were worked to evoke Mihrimah Sultan’s long hair.
Thus two magnificent works of architecture said to be dedicated to one love arose in Istanbul.

The legend’s most moving moment is the meeting of the Sun and the Moon. It is said there is a spot in Istanbul from which both the Edirnekapı and the Üsküdar Mihrimah Sultan mosques can be seen. At the spring equinox, from that point, a crimson sun sets behind the minaret of the Edirnekapı mosque while, at the same moment, the moon rises behind the mosque in Üsküdar.
Mihrimah — Sun and Moon…
The sight inspires wonder. Was it the result of Sinan’s precise calculations, or did a romantic explanation grow around it later?
Whatever the truth may be, this story has become one of Istanbul’s loveliest legends, joining Architect Sinan’s art with the name of Mihrimah Sultan.

items.title: The Advice Fakir Baykurt Never Forgot
items.moral: Moral: Don't kill the "lion" inside a child — his self-confidence — by beating him. True education is not given with fear, but with patience and love.
body: As a child, the Turkish writer Fakir Baykurt (1929–1999) once asked his mother for tea. She took him to Topal Hüseyin’s teahouse and ordered a cup for him.
Eager to drink, he took a large mouthful before realizing how hot it was. Startled by the pain, he dropped the cup.
It fell to the ground without breaking. He expected his mother to slap him, but she simply asked for another cup.
This time, he sipped carefully. For years afterward, he asked why she had not punished him. She never answered.
Much later, his mother, Elif Khanum, visited the village school where he taught. He recalled:
“I became angry during the lesson and shouted at the children. Afterward, I asked, ‘Well, Mother, what did you think of my teaching?’
“‘It wasn’t bad, son.’
“‘The inspectors praise me and give me good marks, and all you say is that it wasn’t bad?’
“She answered, ‘For years you’ve asked why I didn’t slap you over the tea. Now listen.

“‘If I had shouted, the lion inside you would have roared back. If I had beaten you, I might have killed that lion. You might never have become a teacher. Be patient, as I was. Don’t use a stick to kill the courage in these children.’”

items.title: The Road Beyond the Cotton Fields
items.moral: Moral: A teacher not only showed the way to children, but also created new paths for them. For a person who can dream, the world no longer consists of just one path.
body: We could barely read or write when a new teacher came to our village. Aydin became more than a teacher to us; he was like a brother and a father. Seeing our dilapidated school and learning that we expected to spend our lives in the cotton fields brought tears to his eyes.

He asked where one village road led. “To the cotton fields,” we answered. Then he pointed to another road. None of us knew where it went. We had never left the village and knew little of the world beyond it.
That day, he also asked us what we wanted to be when we grew up. We all remained silent because we didn't know what to answer...

He soon taught us to read and write. Then one day, he brought letters from people he said would be our pen pals: doctors, engineers, scientists, and others. For years, these strangers wrote about their work, the meaning of life, and the possibilities opened by education. Until then, none of us had imagined a future beyond growing cotton.
We had believed there was only one road open to us: the road to the fields.
The letters changed that. We began to see where the other road might lead. With Aydin’s help, we continued our studies. Some of us trained as doctors, others as engineers or teachers.
Years later, another letter came to us:
“My children, never stop dreaming. Work hard and keep moving toward your goals. I congratulate you with all my heart. I always knew you could succeed.”
“Your pen pal, Aydin.”
We were astonished. Our own teacher had written all those letters that changed our lives.

items.title: What Is It to Me?
items.moral: Moral: A society weakens when people see injustice and say, “What is it to me?” Indifference allows oppression to grow.
body: Suleiman the Magnificent (1494–1566), who ruled from 1520 until his death, brought the Ottoman state to great power. Yet he sometimes wondered whether the dynasty might one day decline and fall.
He wrote to his foster brother, the scholar Yahya Efendi, whose spiritual insight he respected. “Under what circumstances does a state collapse? Could such a fate await the house of Osman?”
The reply was brief: “What is it to me, my Sultan?”

Reading it at Topkapı Palace, Suleiman was bewildered. Surely Yahya Efendi would not dismiss so serious a question. He went to see him in Beşiktaş. “Brother, please take my letter seriously and give me an answer.”
Yahya Efendi:
“I have, my Sultan. I considered it carefully and gave you my answer.”
“But all you said was, ‘What is it to me?’ You seem to want nothing to do with the matter.”
Yahya Efendi explained:

“When oppression spreads and injustice takes the throne, people ask, ‘What is it to me?’ The shepherds begin devouring the sheep they should protect. Those who know the truth conceal it. The cries of the poor rise to heaven, but no one listens. Then the end is near. The treasury empties, trust disappears, and respect for public order crumbles. That is how a state falls.”
Moved to tears, the sultan bowed his head. He left grateful that someone in his country would speak so plainly to him.
